title: Sum of K Subarrays With Length at Least M
statement:
Choose exactly `k` subarrays (contiguous, non-empty blocks) of the integer array `nums` so that no two of them share a position and each one has at least `m` elements. Return the largest possible total of all the chosen elements.

Positions outside the chosen subarrays are simply left out. The inputs always allow `k` such subarrays.
signature: int maxSum(int[] nums, int k, int m)
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force tries, position by position, to either skip the number or start a subarray there of every allowed length. To organize this, let dp[i][j] be the best total of exactly i subarrays inside the first j numbers. Either number j - 1 is not in the i-th subarray, giving dp[i][j - 1], or the i-th subarray is `nums[s..j - 1]` for some start s with j - s >= m, giving dp[i - 1][s] + prefix[j] - prefix[s]. Trying every s costs O(n) per state. But as j grows by one, exactly one new start, s = j - m, becomes legal, so a running maximum `best` of dp[i - 1][s] - prefix[s] answers that part in O(1).

## Approach

1. `prefix[j]` is the sum of the first j numbers.
2. `previous` holds row i - 1 of the table; row 0 is all zeros (no subarrays, total 0).
3. For each i from 1 to k, fill `current` with -Infinity (not reachable yet), reset `best`, and for j from `i * m` (the shortest prefix that fits i subarrays) to n:
   - admit the start s = j - m: `best = max(best, previous[j - m] - prefix[j - m])`;
   - `current[j] = max(current[j - 1], best + prefix[j])`.
4. After k rows, `previous[n]` is the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

`prefix = [0, 1, 3, 2, 5, 8, 12]`, k = 2, m = 2. Row 1 keeps `best = 0` (start at 0 is best throughout) and becomes `[-∞, -∞, 3, 3, 5, 8, 12]`. Row 2 starts at j = 4: `best = 3 - 3 = 0`, so `current[4] = 5`. At j = 5, start 3 gives `3 - 2 = 1`, so `best = 1` and `current[5] = max(5, 1 + 8) = 9`. At j = 6, `current[6] = max(9, 1 + 12) = 13`: `[1, 2]` plus `[3, 3, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k · n): each row scans the prefixes once.
- Space: O(n): the prefix sums and two rows.

## Pitfalls

- Exactly k subarrays are required, even when every number is negative (Example 2), so unreachable states must be -Infinity, not 0.
- Admit start j - m only when j reaches it; admitting later starts would allow subarrays shorter than m.
- Keep the `current[j - 1]` option, or the i-th subarray is forced to end at the last number of the prefix.
- A full (k + 1) × (n + 1) table can hold 4 million entries; two rows are enough.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prefix` | `prefix[j]` is the sum of `nums[0..j - 1]` |
| `previous`, `current` | rows i - 1 and i: best totals of that many subarrays in each prefix |
| `i`, `j` | the number of subarrays, and the prefix length |
| `best` | the largest `previous[s] - prefix[s]` over the starts s admitted so far |

narration.2: n is the number of values; prefixes have lengths 0 to n.
narration.3: prefix[j] will hold the sum of the first j numbers.
narration.5: Each prefix sum extends the previous one by one number.
narration.7: Row 0 of the table: with no subarrays chosen, every prefix totals 0.
narration.8: Build the row for i subarrays from the row for i - 1.
narration.9: Prefixes that cannot hold i subarrays stay at -Infinity.
narration.10: No start position has been admitted for this row yet.
narration.11: The shortest prefix that can hold i subarrays of length m has i * m numbers.
narration.12: Admit start s = j - m: a subarray beginning there has m numbers by the end of this prefix.
narration.13: Either the i-th subarray ends earlier, or it ends at this prefix's last number and begins at the best admitted start.
narration.15: The finished row becomes the previous row for the next count.
narration.17: The best total of exactly k subarrays in the whole array.
